<reason>Side A controlled the debate by establishing early that existing consumer-protection laws already prohibit hidden paid promotions and buried #ad tags, forcing the clash onto what traditional broadcast-level strictness actually adds. Using the concrete example of a two-year-old gifted microphone on a livestreamer's desk, Side A trapped Side B in a lethal dilemma. Side B first bit the bullet in R1 by insisting that using a free product two years later requires disclosure, then contradicted itself in Pressure Questions by implying two-year-old gifts do not require disclosure on TV, and finally attempted an unconvincing walk-back in R2 while falsely claiming influencers currently face only voluntary guidelines. Side A also thoroughly dismantled Side B's claim that talent agents and contract lawyers can pre-screen hours of unscripted livestreamed conversation like a network standards-and-practices division.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [A3.1] and [A4.1]-[A4.2], Side A exposed Side B's direct contradiction between [B2.3] (insisting that merely using a free microphone for two years requires ongoing disclosure) and [B3.1] (implying broadcast rules do not require disclosing two-year-old gifts), and then caught Side B trying to rewrite [B2.3] in [B4.1] as applying only to active reviews.</best_rebuttal>
